projectDescription: Toxoplasma gondii, a single-celled protozoan parasite (phylum Apicomplexa) and remains the causative pathogen of one of the most wide-spread infectious diseases, toxoplasmosis. To continuously proliferate in warm-blooded animals, this parasite undergoes repeated cycles of invasion, division and induction of host cell rupture. Lactate, which is derived from cellular metabolic pathways, is widely considered not only an energy source in organisms but also a regulatory molecule that participates in gene activation. Lysine lactylation is a new type of protein posttranslational modification (PTM) that was recently associated with chromatin remodeling, but the lysine lactylation of histone and nonhistone proteins has not yet been studied in parasites. To examine the prevalence and function of lactylation in T. gondii parasites, we mapped the lactylation proteome of proliferating tachyzoite cells and found 1,964 lactylation sites on 955 proteins in the T. gondii RH strain. The lactylated proteins were distributed in multiple subcellular compartments and were closely related to a wide variety of biological processes, including mRNA splicing, the citrate cycle (TCA cycle), aminoacyl-tRNA biosynthesis, glyoxylate and dicarboxylate metabolism, glycolysis/gluconeogenesis, oxidative phosphorylation, RNA transport and the HIF-1 signaling pathway. Lysine lactation might regulate numerous cellular processes to aid the establishment of a hospitable environment that allows the survival, replication and dissemination of the parasite. These study offers the first data of the global lactylation proteome and provides a basis for further functional dissection of important proteins associated with T. gondii development and pathogenicity.
dataProcessingProtocol: LC-MS/MS analysis The peptides were dissolved in liquid chromatography mobile phase A (0.1% formic acid mix with 2% acetonitrile) and separated using the EASY-nLC 1000 UPLC system. Mobile phase B was a solution containing 0.1% formic acid and 90% acetonitrile, and during the analysis, the concentration of mobile phase B was increased from 6% to 23% over 26 minutes, from 23% to 35% over 8 minutes and eventually to 80% over 3 minutes. The flow rate throughout the entire process was 600 nL/min. The peptides were processed with an NSI source and then connected to a U Execution Q ExactiveTM Plus instrument (Thermo) for tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS). The electrospray voltage was set to 2.0 kV. The scanning range of the first-level mass spectrometer was 350-1800 m/z, and the scanning resolution was set to 70,000. The fragments were identified at a resolution of 17500 using Orbitrap. An interval of 15.0 seconds was included between one MS scan and the subsequent 20 MS/MS scans. Database search The secondary mass spectrometry data were retrieved using MaxQuant (v1.5.2.8) software from the ToxoDB 46.0 database (8322 sequences, https://toxodb.org/toxo/), and the false positive rate (FDR) caused by random matching through the anti-database was calculated. In addition, the data were passed through a standard contamination library to eliminate the effects of contaminated proteins. Trypsin/P was set as the digestion method, and the maximum of four missed cleavages was allowed. The mass error tolerance of the first search and the main search were set to 20 ppm and 5 ppm, respectively. The mass error tolerance of the secondary fragment ions was 0.02 Da. A carbamidomethyl on cysteine (Cys) was set as a fixed modification, and the variable modifications included oxidation of methionine, acetylation of the N terminus of the protein, and lactylation of lysine. The FDR for protein identification was set to 1%.
sampleProcessingProtocol: Experimental design and statistical rationale The global KLa of soluble proteins derived from the T. gondii RH strain was analyzed by label-free mass spectrometry. Three biological replicates of parasite lactylation were analyzed to evaluate the accuracy of the data obtained in this experiment. A qualitative analysis of lactylation was performed, and Fisher’s exact test was used to determine whether the data were statistically significant. R scripts were used for the statistical tests and pattern generation.  Parasite purification and protein extraction Tachyzoites from peritoneal fluid were filtered through 5.0-μm nucleopore filters and then collected by centrifugation into a centrifuge tube (Guangzhou Jet Bio-Filtration Co., Ltd.). The Percoll (GE Healthcare, Uppsala, Sweden) gradient centrifugation method was used for separation and purification. The purified parasite cells were washed with phosphate-buffered saline (PBS-1X), sonicated three times in lysis buffer (1% protease inhibitor mixture and 8 M urea) using a high-intensity sonicator (Scientz, Ningbo, China). The lysate was centrifuged at 12,000 g (4 °C) for 12 minutes to remove insoluble cell fragments, and the sample concentration was measured using a BCA kit (Beyotime, Shanghai, China).  Trypsin digestion The protein solution was reduced at 56 °C for 30 minutes using 5 mM dithiothreitol and alkylated at 37 °C for 15 minutes using 11 mM iodoacetamide (Sigma, St. Louis, MO, USA) in dark environment. Subsequently, the protein sample was dilated with 100 mM TEAB, and trypsin was added for digestion overnight.  HPLC fractionation Trypsinized peptides were separated by high pH reversed-phase separation (RPF) using a Thermo Betasil C18 column. Within 1 hour, the peptides were divided into 60 fractions, the acetonitrile concentration gradient was divided into 8% to 32% (pH 9.0), and the peptide was then divided into four fractions for in vacuo lyophilization.  Antibody-based PTM enrichment NETN buffer was added to the peptide sample, and the resulting mixture was then mixed with prewashed pan-lysine-lactylation antibody beads (PTM-1401, Hangzhou, China) and incubated overnight at 4 °C. The peptide bonds on the beads were eluted with 0.1% trifluoroacetic acid and dried in vacuo. The resulting peptides were desalted using C18 ZipTip (Millipore) as indicated in the instructions.
